items.title: Weimar Germany had a 'golden' decade — but it was built on US loans
items.claim: Why did Weimar's relative stability (1924-1929) collapse?

options.text: The Dawes Plan (1924) restructured reparations with US loans; the Wall Street Crash (October 1929) collapsed lending; Stresemann had died in October 1929; unemployment hit 6 million by 1932
The British naval blockade resumed in 1927

items.reveal:
The Dawes Plan (1924) and Young Plan (1929) refinanced German reparations through US bank loans. Germany used the loans for infrastructure, social housing and reparations payments — a circular flow.

Gustav Stresemann's diplomacy (Locarno 1925, German League membership 1926) normalised relations with the West. He died on 3 October 1929, three weeks before the Wall Street Crash.

When US loans dried up, German banks failed (Danatbank, July 1931); unemployment soared; the Nazis went from 12 seats (1928) to 230 seats (July 1932), becoming the largest party.
items.why: Weimar's 'collapse' was not inevitable but was structurally vulnerable. The Crash was an external shock that destroyed a recovery dependent on foreign credit — a useful case in how interconnected economies fail.

items.title: Keynes resigned from the British delegation over Versailles
items.claim: What was Keynes's role at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference?

options.text: He helped draft the reparations clauses
He was a British Treasury official; he resigned in June 1919 in protest and published 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace' in December — arguing reparations would devastate Germany and Europe
He was not present at the conference
He represented Lloyd George as foreign affairs adviser

items.reveal:
Keynes was deputy to the British Treasury delegation. His book (December 1919) accused the Big Four — especially Clemenceau and Wilson — of imposing a 'Carthaginian peace' that would ensure future conflict.

The book sold over 100,000 copies and shaped Anglo-American opinion. It helped frame the 1930s 'appeasement' logic — Germany had been wronged at Versailles and deserved revision. Historians (notably Margaret MacMillan, 'Peacemakers' 2001) have argued Keynes overstated reparations' impact: Germany paid only a fraction.

Reparations were formally cancelled in 1932 (Lausanne).
items.why: Keynes's pamphlet is itself a historical event. It shaped the inter-war policy world more than the treaty article it attacked — a reminder that narratives of treaties can matter more than treaty texts.
